segments.translit: sahajānandasundaro hi kṛṣṇācāryyas tam evārthaṃ pratipādayati—
segments.translation: Master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, beautiful with [innate joy]{sahajananda}, sets forth that same meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song by saying that master Kāṇha (Kṛṣṇācārya), beautiful with innate joy, sets forth "that same meaning"; he does not say here what that meaning is (cp.36.m1).

flags.note: The folio mark [৫২ক] (52ka) stands inside the word evārthaṃ in Shastri's edition (tam evā[52ka]rthaṃ). It is not Munidatta's wording: the transliteration joins the word and the translation passes over the mark (cp.36.m1).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has no word for "beautiful" (sundara): lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' bas brjod pa'i phyir, "in order to express it through innate joy". It names the poet nag po glu dbyangs zhabs, taking the name as Kṛṣṇacaryāpāda with caryā as "song" (glu dbyangs), a form the glossary records for Kāṇha elsewhere. Otherwise the introduction agrees (cp.36.m1).
Munidatta's kṛṣṇācārya is rendered "master Kāṇha" so as to keep the approved form of p-kanha while still rendering ācārya, "master" (cp.36.m1, cp.36.m3). See questions.

segments.translit: suna ityādi śūnyam iti| ālokopalabdhisaṃkhyājñānena vāsanāgāraṃ boddhavyaṃ| yogīndreṇa tasya vāsanādoṣaṃ tathatākhaḍgena prahṛtya mohaṃ viṣayāsaṅgalakṣaṇaṃ sakalam ahāritam iti|
segments.translation: "Suna" and so on means "[empty]{sunyata}". The [house]{house} of [habitual tendencies]{vasana} is to be understood through the [knowledge]{jnana} called [culmination of light]{alokopalabdhi}. The [lord of yogis]{yogindra} struck its fault of [habitual tendencies]{vasana} with the [sword]{sword} of [suchness]{tathata}, and [delusion]{moha}, which is marked by attachment to [sense objects]{visaya}, was all carried off.
segments.note: Munidatta glosses suṇa as "empty" and takes the house as the house of habitual tendencies, understood through the knowledge called culmination of light. Where the song strikes with suchness, the lord of yogis strikes its fault of tendencies with the sword of suchness, and all delusion, marked by attachment to sense objects, is carried off (cp.36.m2).

flags.note: For Munidatta's vāsanāgāraṃ boddhavyaṃ, "the house of tendencies is to be understood", the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bag chags la chags par rig par bya'o, "is to be understood as attachment to tendencies": no house, as if reading something like vāsanāsaṅga for vāsanāgāra. Its quotation of line 1a does have a house (stong pa'i khyim), and Munidatta's āgāra supports the draft's "house" for বাহ (cp.36.m2).

Other differences in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293): snang ba thob pa la dgongs pa'i shes pa, "the knowledge that has culmination of light in view", where the Sanskrit has -saṃkhyā-, "called", perhaps reading sandhyā (dgongs pa, as in dgongs pa'i skad); rang bzhin gyi gti mug, "natural delusion", where the Sanskrit has prahṛtya, "having struck", as if reading prakṛti; and gcod pa, "cutting", for ahāritam, "carried off" (cp.36.m2).
tasya vāsanādoṣaṃ may be "its" (the house's) fault of tendencies or "his" (the yogi's); the translation keeps the ambiguous "its" (cp.36.m2).

Munidatta makes delusion itself, not the storehouse, what was "all carried off" (sakalam ahāritam, for saalā ahārī), and gives nothing for lui, "taking", in 1b. His prahṛtya, "having struck", confirms the draft's "Striking" in 1a (cp.36.m2).

Shastri prints ālokopalavdhi-, voddhavyaṃ and tathatākhaṛgena; the transliteration gives -upalabdhi-, boddhavyaṃ and -khaḍgena, since the script does not keep b and v (or ḍ and ṛ) apart and the words are clear.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena dhyānalakṣaṇam āha—
ghumai ṇa ityādi| sahajānandayoganidrā[ṃ] yātī(ntī)ti na cetayati| na tatra bhraṣṭo bhavati| ataeva kṛṣṇācāryyasundaro hi sahajānandayoganidrāluḥ(luṃ)|
tathā ca dvikalpe|
ghumai garuṇaha bhakṣaṇe ityādi|
tasyāṃ sahajānandanidrāyāṃ|
segments.translation:
With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he states the defining mark of [concentration]{dhyana}:
"He sleeps and is not…" and so on. He goes into the [yogic sleep]{yoganidra} of [innate joy]{sahajananda}, and so he is not aware. He does not fall away from it. Therefore the beautiful master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} is indeed a sleeper in the yogic sleep of innate joy.
And so in the [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}:
"He sleeps, eating poisons," and so on.
In that [sleep]{nidra} of innate joy.
segments.note: Munidatta says the refrain gives the defining mark of concentration. Its sleep is the yogic sleep of innate joy: going into it, Kāṇha is not aware, yet does not fall away from it, and so he is a sleeper in that yogic sleep. He backs this with a line on sleeping from the Dvikalpa, the Hevajra (cp.36.m3).

equations.en: goes into the yogic sleep of innate joy (sahajānandayoganidrāṃ yāti)
a sleeper in the yogic sleep of innate joy (sahajānandayoganidrālu)

citations.quoted: ghumai garuṇaha bhakṣaṇe ityādi ("He sleeps, eating poisons," and so on)

flags.note: yātī(ntī)ti: Shastri's (ntī) proposes yāntīti. I read yātīti, yāti iti, "he goes … and so", which suits the singular subject; the Tibetan gnyid du song ste, "having gone into sleep", supports a verb of going (cp.36.m3).
sahajānandayoganidrāluḥ(luṃ): Shastri suggests the accusative -luṃ; I keep the nominative, as predicate of kṛṣṇācāryyasundaraḥ (cp.36.m3).

In the Dvikalpa line, garuṇaha is unclear. The translation follows the Tibetan, gnyid yur dug rnams za bar byed, "sleeping, he eats poisons", which points to a word for poison (gara, garala); garuḍa, the snake-eating bird, is also conceivable. I have not been able to place the line in the Hevajra Tantra (cp.36.m3).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) differs in detail: khyod la sems med pa, "you have no mind", for na cetayati; rnal 'byor pas, "by the yogin", for -yoga-; brjid pa'i phyir, "because he is majestic", taking sundaro hi as a reason; and, for the closing locative, de'i lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba gnyid do, "its innate joy is sleep", a statement where the Sanskrit has a fragment (cp.36.m3).
tasyāṃ sahajānandanidrāyāṃ, "in that sleep of innate joy", stands alone; it seems to gloss the sleeping of the quoted line, and is translated as a fragment (cp.36.m3).

Munidatta gives no gloss of saparabibhāgā, "the division of self and other" (2a), and nothing clear for lāṅgā (2b, "sunk" in the draft); his "beautiful" (sundara) may stand where lāṅgā stood, or may simply be his epithet for Kāṇha, as in cp.36.m1 (cp.36.m3).

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena tam evāha—
na cittacetanāvikalpo bodhinādya te| ataeva tena jñānena| sakalam iti trailokyaṃ pariśodhya nirbharaṃ yathā bhavati tathā jñānanidrāṃ gataḥ|
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he states the same:
There is no [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of [mind]{citta} and [awareness]{cetana}; ⟨[feeling]{vedana}, too, is without conceptual thought⟩. Therefore, by that [knowledge]{jnana} ("everything" means the [three worlds]{trailokya}), having purified them, he went fully into the [sleep]{nidra} of knowledge.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as restating the refrain: there is no conceptual thought of mind and awareness (the next words are damaged; the Tibetan adds that feeling too is nonconceptual). "Everything" is the three worlds: having purified them by that knowledge, Kāṇha went fully into the sleep of knowledge (cp.36.m4).

flags.note: bodhinādya te is damaged and gives no sense. Since the song pairs ceaṇa with beana, and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) goes on tshor ba yang de rnam par mi rtog pa'o, "feeling, too, is nonconceptual in the same way", these words probably glossed beana: perhaps vedanādyās te, "nor feeling and the rest" (বোধিনাদ্য for বেদনাদ্য is a small change). The words in angle brackets are supplied from the Tibetan, not read in the Sanskrit (cp.36.m4).

Where the Sanskrit pairs mind and awareness (cittacetanāvikalpa) for ceaṇa, the Tibetan glosses with sems, "mind", alone (sems med ces pa ni sems kyi rnam par mi rtog pa'o) and then with tshor ba, "feeling", for beana, following its own line (sems med tshor ba med par). It also takes nirbharaṃ with the purifying (shin tu yongs su sbyangs pas, "thoroughly purified") and renders yathā bhavati tathā word for word (ji lta ba bzhin du gyur pa) (cp.36.m4).

pariśodhya, "having purified", stands where 3b has suphala kari, "making fruitful" in the draft; the Tibetan line has grol bar byas, "freed". Munidatta does not gloss suphala. His nirbharaṃ, "full", seems to echo the bhara of 3a ("deep" in the draft), and is rendered "fully" (cp.36.m4).
ataeva tena jñānena, "therefore, by that knowledge", stands as a fragment; I construe it with pariśodhya, as the Tibetan does (de'i ye shes kyi …) (cp.36.m4).

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena svapratibhāsajñānam āha—
svapanetyādi| avaṇāgavanam iti pūrvvoktakrameṇa candrasūryyayor yātāyātaṃ khaṇḍayitvā| ghāniketi| avadhūtikāpavanañ ca sahajānanda[ṃ] praveśayitvā| may[ā] svapnavat tribhuvanaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ śūnyañ ca|
tathā cāgamaḥ|
yathā kumārī svapnāntareṣu sā putra[ṃ] jāta[ṃ] mṛtañ ca paśyati| jāte 'pi tuṣṭā mṛte daurmmanaskā evaṃ jānītha sarvvadharmmān|
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he states the [knowledge]{jnana} of what [appears]{abhasa} to oneself:
"In a [dream]{svapna}…" and so on. "[Coming and going]{coming-and-going}": having cut off, by the process described before, the [coming and going]{coming-and-going} of the [moon]{moon} and the [sun]{surya}. "Ghānika": having also made the [wind]{vayu} of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} enter [innate joy]{sahajananda}. I saw the [three worlds]{trailokya} as like a dream, and [empty]{sunyata}.
And so the [scripture]{agama} says:
"As a young girl in her [dreams]{svapna} sees a son born and dead, delighted when he is born and dejected when he dies, so know all [dharmas]{dharma}."
segments.note: Munidatta calls the couplet the knowledge of what appears to oneself. "Coming and going" is the moon and sun's coming and going, cut off; the word he cites as ghānika is making the wind of the avadhūtī, the central channel, enter innate joy. Then the three worlds are seen as like a dream, and empty (cp.36.m5).

equations.en: the coming and going of the moon and the sun, cut off
having made the wind of the avadhūtī enter innate joy

citations.quoted: yathā kumārī svapnāntareṣu sā putraṃ jātaṃ mṛtañ ca paśyati| jāte 'pi tuṣṭā mṛte daurmanaskā evaṃ jānītha sarvadharmān ("As a young girl in her dreams sees a son born and dead … so know all dharmas")

flags.note: Munidatta cites the first word of 4b as ghānika, not the song's ghoria. His gloss, making the wind enter innate joy, suits a sense like "mixed" or "pressed" (compare Bengali ghāni, "oil press"). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'dres par byas nas, "having mixed", in the line and 'dres mar byas pa in the comment. The draft's "churned up" is compatible; "mixed" is the alternative (cp.36.m5).

For Munidatta's svapratibhāsajñāna, "the knowledge of what appears to oneself", the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rang gi dgongs pa'i ye shes, "the wisdom of his own intent", as if reading a word for intention (abhiprāya, sandhi) in place of pratibhāsa (cp.36.m5).

Munidatta has svapnavat, "like a dream", where line 4a has sbapaṇe, "in a dream" (so the draft): for him the three worlds are dreamlike, not seen in a dream. The Tibetan comment agrees (bdag gi rmi lam dang 'dra bar); the Tibetan line has rmi lam na, "in the dream". The comment is translated as it stands and the draft is left alone (cp.36.m5).
Munidatta spells the song's abaṇā gamaṇa as avaṇāgavana, and glosses it before ghānika, reversing the order of the line (cp.36.m5).

avadhūtikāpavana may be "the wind of the avadhūtī" or "the avadhūtī and the wind". The Tibetan makes the avadhūtī the place the wind enters (a wa d+hU tIr rlung dang lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba la rab tu zhugs pa'i phyir). The folio mark [৫৩] inside the compound is dropped; Shastri's restorations [ṃ] and [ā] (the input transliteration leaves a Bengali vowel sign in maya[া]) are kept in brackets (cp.36.m5).

segments.translit:
caturthapadena vajragurumāhātmyam āha—
śākhi karītyādi| śrīgurujālandharipādān yasmi[n] dharmme sākṣiṇaḥ kṛtvā teṣāṃ pā[dā]bjareṇugaṇaprasādāt| ye ye pustakadṛṣṭigatāḥ paṇḍitācāryyāḥ| te te mama pāśasānnidhānāntaram api na paśyanti|| 36||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states the [greatness]{mahatmya} of the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru}:
"I will make … my [witness]{saksin}" and so on. In the [dharma]{dharma} in which I have made the glorious [guru]{guru} [Jālandharipāda]{p-jalandhari} witness, by the [grace]{prasada} of the many grains of dust of his lotus feet, whatever [paṇḍita]{pandita} teachers there are whose sight goes no further than books, they do not see even the space near my side. (36)
segments.note: Munidatta says the couplet states the greatness of the vajra guru (vajra: the tantric emblem of the indestructible). Kāṇha makes the glorious guru Jālandharipāda witness; by the grace of the dust of his feet, paṇḍita teachers (learned scholars) whose sight goes no further than books do not see even the space near his side (cp.36.m6).

flags.note: In pāśasānnidhāna, pāśa is pārśva, "side" (it stands for the song's pākhi), not pāśa, "noose": "the nearness of my side". The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bdag gi rtsa bar, "near me", and its line bdag gis rtsar; neither has zhags pa, "noose" (cp.36.m6).

Munidatta keeps the witness of 5a: sākṣiṇaḥ kṛtvā, "having made [him] witnesses" (an honorific plural, rendered "witness"). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads mngon sum, "directly evident", as if from sākṣāt: its line has "made directly evident from Jālandhara's feet", and its comment has the guru make the nature of things (chos nyid, for dharma) directly evident to the poet (gang la chos nyid mngon sum du mdzad pa). The two do not say the same thing (cp.36.m6).

রাহঅ in 5b: Munidatta's verb is na paśyanti, "do not see", so he takes the word as a verb of looking or seeing, which supports the draft's "do not look my way"; the Tibetan line agrees (lta mi byed). Nothing in his wording reflects "stay" (Bengali rah-), though "not even the space near my side" keeps the sense of distance. The draft is left as it is (cp.36.m6).
The Tibetan has chu skyes kyi rdul la reg pa'i drin, "the kindness of touching the dust of the lotus", where the Sanskrit has -reṇugaṇa-, "the many grains of dust" (cp.36.m6).

yasmi[n] dharmme has no correlative; I take it as "the dharma in which", with the paṇḍitas' failure to see as the main clause. The Tibetan also has a relative (gang la). [n] and [dā] are Shastri's restorations; ॥ ৩৬ ॥ is the song number, kept as "(36)" (cp.36.m6).

proposals.definition: Side, flank (Sanskrit pārśva). Munidatta writes pāśa, a Prakrit-like form of pārśva, in "the nearness of my side", his rendering of the poet's side in song 36, 5b (cp.36.m6); elsewhere he has pārśvastha, "standing at the side" (cp.33.m2). The Tibetan has rtsa bar, "near". Not pāśa, "noose", nor pakṣa, "side".
proposals.rationale: Munidatta's pāśa (cp.36.m6) looks like pāśa, "noose", which the glossary lists under noose; an entry keeps later drafters from reading "noose" there. The song's own pākhi (5b) may come from pakṣa, so it is left out of the forms until you decide between this entry and paksa.

questions: Names in the commentary: Munidatta's kṛṣṇācārya is rendered "master Kāṇha" (cp.36.m1, cp.36.m3) to keep the approved form while rendering ācārya, and his "Dvikalpa" is rendered with the approved "Hevajra" (cp.36.m3). Would you rather list "Kṛṣṇācārya" as a variant of p-kanha and "Dvikalpa" as a variant of tx-hevajra for commentary use?

cp.36.m4: bodhinādya te is damaged. I have supplied the Tibetan's "feeling, too, is without conceptual thought" in angle brackets ⟨ ⟩ and suggested vedanādyās te as the underlying reading. Is the angle-bracket convention acceptable for supplied text, or should the gap be left with only a note?

4b ghoria: Munidatta cites ghānika and glosses it as making the wind enter innate joy, and the Tibetan line and comment have "having mixed" (cp.36.m5). The draft's "churned up" is compatible; do you want "mixed" considered for the line?

4a: Munidatta reads "like a dream" (svapnavat) where the draft has "In a dream" (cp.36.m5); 3b: neither witness supports "making fruitful" (Munidatta has pariśodhya, "having purified", cp.36.m4; the Tibetan line has grol bar byas, "freed"). I have left the draft alone; do these want notes on the lines?
5b রাহঅ: Munidatta's na paśyanti, "do not see" (cp.36.m6), and the Tibetan lta mi byed both support the draft's "look"; I see no ground in either for "stay". Agreed?

Citations: the verse of the girl who dreams of a son born and dead (cp.36.m5) is, I believe, from the Samādhirāja Sūtra, which Munidatta calls only "scripture"; it is marked not confident. I could not place the Dvikalpa line ghumai garuṇaha bhakṣaṇe (cp.36.m3) in the Hevajra Tantra, and its garuṇaha is translated from the Tibetan ("poisons"). Please check both.

Markup of inflected forms: I have marked "empty" with sunyata (cp.36.m2, cp.36.m5) and "appears" with abhasa (cp.36.m5), since the glossary's forms list those very Sanskrit words. Acceptable, or should only the exact English be marked?
Proposal parsva ("side"): offered so that Munidatta's pāśa (cp.36.m6) is not taken for "noose". If you prefer, it could instead be folded into paksa ("side") with a note there.
